title: TB9-17710
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellants) are citizens of India appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) that they are neither "Convention refugee(s)" nor "person(s) in need of protection".
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellants) are citizens of India appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) that they are neither "Convention refugee(s)" nor "person(s) in need of protection".
I allow this appeal, set aside the determination of the RPD and am substituting with my own determination. The Appellants are "Convention refugee(s)".1
Based on my review of the evidence in the file, I conclude that the RPD member erred in her determination of a viable internal flight alternative (IFA) in Mumbai, Hyderabad, Bangalore, and Kolkata.

I find that the XXXX would be at risk from members of the Vishva Hindu Parishad (VHP) party if they relocated to Mumbai, Hyderabad, Bangalore, or Kolkata, or anywhere else in India, because of their interfaith marriage, and that they would not receive adequate protection from the police. Background2

The Appellants all relied on Mr. XXXXBOC narrative and the testimony of both Mr. and Mrs. XXXX. In summary, Mr. XXXXis a Muslim man who fears members of the VHP, a right-wing Hindu extremist group. This group targeted Mr. XXXXbecause of his marriage to a Hindu woman, Mrs. XXXX. In addition, the XXXXare claiming persecution by Indian society on the grounds of being Muslim in India and as a result of their interfaith marriage.
Mr. XXXX was named as the designated representative for his minor daughters, XXXX and XXXX, before the RPD, and this designation was confirmed by the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD).
The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration Canada (the Minister) intervened before the RPD by filing submissions and documents on credibility, but has not intervened in this appeal.
The XXXX submit that the RAD should apply the correctness standard of review.3

I agree with the XXXX. When reviewing the RPD decision, I am required to independently assess all the evidence and determine whether the RPD was correct in relation to each alleged error of law, fact or mixed fact and law. 4 ANALYSIS OF THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL Discrimination not amounting to persecution5

The RPD's finding that the discrimination that Mr. and Mrs. XXXX said they experienced from family members and Indian society in general due to their interfaith marriage did not rise to the level of persecution is correct.
Mr. XXXX testified that there was resistance from both their extended family and society, which made them feel unwelcome. He also explained that he had been discriminated against in the workplace.
The RPD analyzed this part of the claim distinctly from the XXXX fear of the VHP party members. As will be discussed below, her IFA analysis focussed on the XXXX fear of VHP party members.

The RPD found that Mr. XXXX testimony regarding feelings of resistance from family members and society and the absence of invitations "to a lot of social gatherings" did not cumulatively rise to the level of persecution, as those acts were not violations of basic human rights.

Mr. XXXX also alleged that he was discriminated by employers because of his religious profile as a Muslim. He testified that he was not given an opportunity to interview for "a couple of jobs" because the selectors were not Muslim and "probably put [my application] in the trash". He also testified that he would have received more help from the police in India if he did not have a Muslim name.

The RPD found Mr. XXXX allegations that he was refused job interviews and police assistance because of his last name, speculative, and therefore, not sufficient to establish a serious possibility of persecution.

The XXXX argue in appeal that the RPD erred by misunderstanding the heart of their claim by presuming that the basis of their claim consisted of their family's opinion of their interfaith marriage. They add that the RPD erred by focussing on supplementary issues such as experiences of being discriminated against within the work force and barred from being allowed the opportunity for a job interview.

The XXXX further argue that the RPD failed to adequately address, by way of assessment, the incidents that had occurred against Mr. XXXX by an active and powerful political party, working under the very government in which the RPD expected Mr. XXXX to seek protection from. According to the XXXX, the correct assessment would be of their fear of being persecuted as a result of a national Hindu movement against Muslims. They add that an individualized assessment of their claim was not done.

In my opinion, the RPD did not fail to assess the XXXX primary fear of VHP party members and their fear of being persecuted as a result of a national Hindu movement against Muslims. The RPD member was not wrongly dwelling on supplementary fears, she simply analyzed them separately.

By focussing her decision on a forward-looking assessment of a viable IFA, while considering the VHP party members as the persecutors, she accepted the XXXX allegations of past attacks and threats as credible. I disagree with the XXXX assertion that the RPD ignored the ultimate core of the claim. The RPD proceeded with a forward-looking analysis to determine whether an IFA was possible, given the past persecution by VHP members.

I agree with the RPD's conclusion that the behaviours described by the XXXX, whether by their family members or in Mr. XXXX work life and his experience with the police in New Delhi, were discriminatory but that they did not cumulatively rise to the level of persecution.
The RPD's assessment on this part of the claim is correct. The RPD erred in assessing the viability of an IFA in Mumbai, Hyderabad, Bangalore, and Kolkata

In my opinion, the RPD was incorrect in her IFA assessment. The XXXX do not have an IFA in the cities of Mumbai, Hyderabad, Bangalore, and Kolkata or elsewhere in India because there is a serious possibility that they will be persecuted based on their religion and interfaith marriage.

This assessment is based on a two-prong test. Once the IFA has been raised, the onus of proof is on the Appellants to establish that: 1) there is a serious possibility that they will be persecuted in the part of the country identified as an IFA or that on a balance of probabilities, they would be subjected personally to a danger of torture or to a risk to their lives or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in the IFA; 2) the conditions in that part of the country must be such that it would be objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the Appellants, for them to seek refuge there.6

The National Documentation Package (NDP) on India has been updated since the RPD hearing in this file, and I will consider the updated information, especially on the country conditions with respect to Hindu extremism, in regards to my forward-looking analysis of the XXXX risk and the availability of an IFA.
I advised the XXXX that I would be analyzing IFA, specifically in Mumbai, Hyderabad, Bangalore, and Kolkata, as well as state protection. I disclosed the latest NDP and requested further submissions.

They responded to my request and filed supplementary submissions and documentation on October 25, 2019.7 These will be addressed further below. First prong- The Possibility of Persecution in the Proposed IFAs8

The RPD found that the XXXX did not face a serious possibility of persecution in Mumbai, Hyderabad, Bangalore, or Kolkata because the VHP members that attacked Mr. XXXX would not find them there due to the country's large population and geography. She added that the VHP would be hard pressed to know where to begin to look. She specified that the VHP would not have the means to locate them outside of New Delhi.
Mr. XXXX had testified that the VHP organization was widely based and had a large network of members throughout the country, who give any information they have to the offices of the VHP.

The RPD did not find that this meant that the VHP had the ability or the resources to locate the XXXX all over India. She referred to a UK Country Guidance report that stated that it would be difficult for the police, or anyone, to track an individual in another state to which they had fled.
The RPD also found that the XXXX had not established that the VHP would be motivated to locate them outside of New Delhi.

Mr. XXXXhad testified that after the first attack against him, on XXXX XXXX, 2018, and after he moved his family from New Delhi to South Delhi, a VHP member had called him and told him he knew where they had relocated to and that they could not hide from the VHP. Mr. XXXX also testified that his cousin told him VHP members were seen around their house in XXXX 2018. The RPD member noted that the XXXX were never approached in South Delhi, and that this further failed to establish that the VHP would be able to locate them in one of the proposed IFAs.

In addition, the RPD also noted that Mr. XXXX was unaware of anyone looking for them in New Delhi since XXXX of 2018 and found that this pointed to a lack of desire on the part of the VHP to track them elsewhere in India.
Based on the above, the RPD concluded that the XXXX would not face a serious possibility of persecution in the proposed IFAs.

In their memorandum of appeal, the XXXX argue that the proposed IFAs do not mitigate the fact that the VHP has the resources to find and locate them. They ask that the widespread corruption, bribery involved within the system and the VHP's strong-willed movement to kill Muslims, by way of Love Jihad, be considered.

Love Jihad was described before the RPD as a movement (Love Jihad, also called Romeo Jihad, is an unsubstantiated campaign defined as an activity under which Muslim men target women belonging to non-Muslim communities for conversion to Islam by feigning love) where they target Muslim men who marry Hindu women and try to eliminate Muslim men.9

There were several articles in evidence put forth by the XXXX, before the RPD, on the VHP Party, their actions against Muslims and the systematic racism against Muslims in India which is not being stopped by the authorities, as well as the concept of Love Jihad and interfaith marriage.10

In the supplementary submissions that I received, the XXXX refer to the country report that the RPD relied on to show that it was difficult for anyone to be tracked in India and argue that this was similar to the country information that supported an IRB jurisprudential guide that has since been revoked. They add that the reason it was revoked was because of developments in the country information, such as information on connectivity between police forces in India.

The XXXX argue that because of the Love Jihad phenomenon in India, they will not be safe anywhere, as Muslim men are being targeted for luring Hindu women, and Mr. XXXX has been personally attacked and threatened because of this in the past. They submit that this is even more so because the VHP has close ties with the ruling political party.

The XXXX also argued that because of a recent citizenship amendment in India, Muslims are being stripped of their Indian citizenship. They submit information and documentation about legislative attempts to isolate Muslims, which are being pushed through by the current political party, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). As such, they argue that should they return to India, they will face possible exclusion and loss of their citizenship.

The supplementary documentation submitted by the XXXX, with their submissions dated October 25, 2019, is accepted as new evidence before the RAD as, in my opinion, it meets the criteria of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA and more precisely, is evidence that I requested when I asked for additional submissions on IFA and state protection. As such, the XXXX could not have been expected to produce it before the RPD. It is new information that is relevant to the issues of IFA and state protection in this claim, which are determinative, and the documents appear to come from credible sources.
I have considered the updated research and information contained in the most current NDP, as well as the XXXX submissions and supporting documents.

In essence, the XXXX are arguing that the reason they will be located, wherever they go, is because of becoming a target of the VHP because of their interfaith marriage, and the fact that they are all now Muslim. Mrs. XXXX was Hindu and she converted for her marriage.

Mr. XXXX was first threatened over this on XXXX XXXX, 2018, but he managed to drive away. On XXXX XXXX, 2018, Mr. XXXX was physically attacked and beaten until he fell unconscious and required medical treatment. Mr. XXXX tried to report the matter to the police and he was rebuffed. The police refused to take his complaint saying that this was common and they did not have time to waste on such matters.

In my opinion, although this is a problem that began in New Delhi, there is evidence that the XXXX have been identified by members of the VHP and that there is a hit list circulating on social media encouraging Hindu extremists to hunt down interfaith couples in India.11

I agree with the XXXX that the country documentation relied on by the RPD about the difficulties in tracking an individual in India is similar to a line of reasoning found in the IRB jurisprudential guide that has been revoked. There are other sources in the NDP that refute this idea and the information we have on the ability for authorities to communicate in India has evolved.

The country documentation also reveals that corruption is rife within police forces in India and this leads to the conclusion that an individual could be tracked, depending on who was searching and if they could access the authorities' database.12

Given the XXXX interfaith marriage and that Mr. XXXX received threats in person and by phone by members of the VHP, even after having relocated from New Delhi to South Delhi, and given the size, nature and connections of the VHP party, coupled with the current anti-Muslim sentiment in India which is being advanced by the current political party in power, I conclude that there is a serious possibility that this family could face persecution based on their religion, even if they were to relocate to one of the proposed IFAs, or elsewhere in India.
The RPD's decision on this part of the IFA analysis was incorrect. Second prong-Relocation to the Proposed IFAs Is Reasonable13

In my opinion, because the XXXX have established a serious possibility of persecution in Mumbai, Hyderabad, Bangalore, and Kolkata, and elsewhere in India under the first prong of the IFA test, it is not necessary to pursue with an analysis under the second prong.
As a result, there is no IFA in India for the XXXX.
There is a presumption that a state is willing and able to adequately protect its citizens.

The XXXX fear the VHP party, and Mr. XXXX was threatened and attacked in XXXX 2018 by members of this party on two separate occasions. The police refused to take his complaint or take any action to assist him.
The RPD found, within her IFA analysis, that adequate state protection existed in India for religious minorities.

In their memorandum of appeal, the XXXX argued that state protection cannot be determined in a vacuum. The willingness and ability of states to protect their citizens may be linked to the nature of the persecution in question.

The XXXX submit that the VHP is not an ordinary person or group that can be tamed. Rather, this group is working hand in hand with the current government in power, the BJP, which is made up of Hindu nationalists and wish to wipe Muslims out of India. It is unreasonable to expect the victims of the system, of the government, to turn to the very authority that is stripping them of their human rights.

The XXXX add that the presumption that they can seek protection in other areas of the country is not an adequate recourse as they have fully addressed their level of subjective and objective fear that forcing them to return to a country where they have proven fear of death by the Indian government is against their Charter rights.

In the supplementary submissions that I received, the XXXX again argue that they fear the VHP because of its close ties to the ruling BJP party. As a result, their agents of persecution should be considered as Indian state actors. They add that in 2018 the CIA in the U.S. classified the VHP as a militant religious organization.
The XXXX say that because the VHP are state actors, they have rebutted the presumption of state protection.

Although I would not go so far as to say that the VHP are state actors, it is clear from the documentary evidence that there is a strong connection between the VHP and the ruling political party, the BJP.

More to the point, Mr. XXXX attempted to file complaints with the police and was rebuffed and insulted. The police superior said this was a useless incident that was common and that they did not have time to waste on such reports.
In my opinion, there can be no state protection for the XXXX in India as they have already tried to seek protection and were dismissed without any action taken to help them.

I also find that given the current political climate in India as reported in the XXXX supporting documents as well as sources in the NDP reporting on mixed marriages, police corruption and impunity throughout India, it is more than likely that the XXXX would not receive adequate state protection elsewhere in India if they relocated.14
In other words, the XXXX have rebutted the presumption of state protection for New Delhi, Mumbai, Hyderabad, Bangalore, and Kolkata, as well as for the rest of India.
My analysis of the evidence reveals that the RPD erred and was incorrect in her determination of a viable IFA.

The XXXX have established that there is a serious possibility of persecution by members of the VHP if they relocated to Mumbai, Hyderabad, Bangalore, and Kolkata, or elsewhere in India, based on their religion, and that the police would not provide adequate state protection.

For all these reasons, I allow this appeal, set aside the determination of the RPD and am substituting with my own determination that XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXXand XXXX XXXX XXXXare "Convention refugee(s)". 15 Julie Corry Me Julie Corry November 18, 2019 Date JC/lp 1 Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), S.C. 2001, c. 27, s. 96, and 111(1)(b). 2 Appellants' Basis of Claim forms, including a narrative, pages 14-73 of the RPD record (BOC); RPD reasons and decision, dated June 14, 2019, at para. 2, page 4 of the RPD record (RPD Reasons). 3 Appellants' memorandum, pp. 22-23 of the appeal record. 4 Minister of Citizenship and Immigration v.
